summary: A collection of enka songs with travelling and period-story themes, including “Meigetsu Akagiyama”, “Ruten” and “Akagi no Komoriuta”. The source listing documents a later export pressing of the same programme; the pressing of this copy still needs confirmation.
This twelve-song collection pairs the title song with “Jūroku no Koi”, “Mineko no Komoriuta” and “Furusato Koiuta”, drawing on enka and kayōkyoku repertoire.

A Japanese song collection by Chieko Baisho, presented with a cherry-blossom portrait sleeve. The photographed cover is the identification source here: its full title and exact edition still need confirmation.
A twelve-track album built around songs of separation, including the title track, “Kyoto kara Hakata made” and “Ryōta no Komoriuta”. Released by RCA in 1972.
Honda’s 1971 folk and popular-song album includes “Aru Asa Umarete”, “Kibō no Kuni” and the title song “Ieji”. The sleeve presents it under the English title Going Home.

The sleeve presents this collection as Harumi Miyako’s Nagashiuta / Miryoku no Subete. Its red-kimono portrait distinguishes it from the other Nagashiuta record in this collection; the exact edition remains unidentified.
A fourteen-song selection spanning “Osaka Shigure”, “Kita no Yado kara” and “Suki ni Natta Hito”. This is the AX-7293 collection, distinct from the other Best Album sleeve on these shelves.
Sixteen enka selections, opening with “Uminari no Uta” and “Kita no Yado kara”. The programme also includes “Namida no Renrakusen” and “Anko Tsubaki wa Koi no Hana”.
A two-record selection of twenty-four songs, including “Hitorine no Komoriuta”, “Sensō wa Shiranai” and “Toki ni wa Haha no Nai Ko no Yō ni”. Released on Polydor in 1970.
A family-oriented collection of familiar international songs. Its twelve selections include “Do-Re-Mi”, “Please Mr. Postman”, “Jambalaya” and “Over the Rainbow”.
A twelve-song selection in CBS/Sony’s Gift Pack Series, bringing together “Shiroi Hana”, “Mimi o Sumashite Goran” and “Aki demo nai noni”.
A collection of enduring folk songs, including “Hitori no Te”, “Tōi Sekai ni” and “Kyō no Hi wa Sayōnara”. The title track opens this 1971 CBS/Sony album.
Volume three of a koto collection devoted to compositions by Michio Miyagi. The sleeve credits performers including Kiyoko Miyagi and Kazue Miyagi, and lists “Haru no Umi” among the works.
A selection of twelve songs, including “Jūsan’ya”, “Atooi Shamisen”, “Gion Kouta” and “Tenryū Kudareba”. The programme draws on Japanese traditional and popular-song repertoire.
Released on 5 March 1971, this is the third album in Sony’s official Red Birds discography. It sits between Red Birds and Takeda no Komoriuta in the group’s early recording history.

Originally released on 10 April 1978, this nine-track album opens with the spoken “Genki Desu ka” and includes “Wakareuta”, “Keshō” and “Sejō”. This collection holds the C28A0146 reissue; its pressing date is still unconfirmed.
Iruka’s JULIA is represented here by the PANAM GWP-1019 LP. The artist’s official discography documents the album alongside her wider recording catalogue.
A twelve-song folk album by Wish, ending with “Rokugatsu no Komoriuta”. Other selections include “Kazaguruma”, “Tegami” and “Shihatsu Ressha de”.
A ten-song album from 1983, closing with its title song, “Umi no Mieru Heya”. The programme also includes “Watashi wa Ima”, “Shabon-dama” and “Room Mirror”.
The Columbia sleeve identifies this as Chiyoko Shimakura’s Aishōshū, a collection of favourite songs. The visible catalogue number is ALS-5027; the release year still needs confirmation.
A vocal jazz set mixing standards and contemporary songs, from “How About You?” and “These Foolish Things” to Stevie Wonder’s “Too Shy to Say”. Released by Philips in 1980.

This two-record collection gathers twenty-four songs, including “Jūshichi no Natsu”, “Hajimete no Dekigoto” and “Watashi no Aoi Tori”. It is Junko Sakurada’s edition of Victor’s Best Collection ’76 series.
A two-record Ayumi Ishida collection in Columbia’s Green & Glorious 3000 series. The obi advertises songs including “Blue Light Yokohama” and “Taiyō wa Naiteiru”.

A Harumi Miyako compilation titled Best Album, identifiable here by its blue blossom border. Its precise catalogue number and programme still need checking, so it is kept separate from the AX-7293 compilation.
A twenty-four-song, two-record anthology including “Coffee Rumba”, “Tokyo Blues” and “Akashia no Ame ga Yamu Toki”. The title translates approximately as Love, Affection, and Tears.
A lullaby programme combining Japanese songs with international selections such as “Hushabye Mountain”, “Summertime” and “Hush Little Baby”. Released on Philips in 1968.
Yamagata’s debut album, originally released on 25 March 1973 when she was sixteen. Its folk repertoire includes “Kaze ni Fukarete Ikō”, “Akai Hana Shiroi Hana” and “Mayonaka no Guitar”.

Recorded at Tokyo’s Sankei Hall on 27 October 1969, this recital pairs Ishida’s songs with film themes and international favourites. Selections include “Blue Light Yokohama”, “Scarborough Fair” and “The Shadow of Your Smile”.
Nishida interprets twelve Japanese lyrical songs, including “Hamabe no Uta”, “Kōjō no Tsuki”, “Hana” and the title piece. The collection was issued by Polydor in 1970.
An enka album led by “Omoide-zake”, alongside interpretations of “Tsugaru Kaikyō Fuyugeshiki”, “Kita no Yado kara” and “Kitaguni no Haru”. Released in 1979.

The second volume of Uta wa Waga Inochi, presented in a blue Columbia sleeve. The photographed copy identifies Hibari Misora and catalogue ALS-5059; the sleeve is retained as the primary identification source.
A Victor album bearing the title “Anata ni Ageru”. The photographed sleeve confirms Mineko Nishikawa and catalogue SJX-198, with a close-up portrait and pink title panel.

Originally issued on 25 February 1980, this twelve-song album opens with “Osaka Shigure” and includes “Sayonara Kaikyō” and “Harumi”. Columbia’s official reissue page confirms the original AX-7226 catalogue number.
Mineko Nishikawa’s two-record contribution to Victor’s Best Collection ’76 series. Its SJV-836–7 catalogue number distinguishes it from Junko Sakurada’s similarly titled set.
A twelve-track collection led by “Kanashimi no Machi”, with “Onna no Melody” and “Ai no Kodoku”. This RCA issue uses the CD-4 four-channel format advertised as QuadraDisc on the sleeve.

A two-record Hibari Misora collection in the Golden Star Deluxe series. The photographed sleeve confirms AB-7001–2; the detailed programme is awaiting verification rather than borrowing another singer’s track list.
A Sony demonstration record promoting SQ four-channel sound, under the title Chikyū wa Hitotsu (“The Earth Is One”). The exact edition and performers are still being checked.
Sony’s official discography dates Studio Live to 20 December 1971, following Takeda no Komoriuta. It is an early Red Birds release, distinct from the later Million People concert album.
A two-record Red Birds compilation issued as Golden Disk. The orange-bordered sleeve identifies catalogue ETP-60223–24; its release year remains unconfirmed.

The second volume of Shizue Sasagawa’s Aiginshū, a collection of gin’ei vocal performances. The moon-and-blossom sleeve supplies the artist and volume identification; a release date and full programme remain unverified.
A nagauta performance of Shinkyoku Urashima, divided into two parts across the record’s sides. The Columbia release credits Ijūrō Yoshimura and shamisen player Eijirō Kineya.
